paragraphs: MAIA investigates whether a neural model can help explain the internal behavior of other neural models. It gives a pretrained vision-language model tools for running interpretability experiments, turning explanation into an iterative process of proposing tests, examining responses, and describing what those responses suggest about a model component.

The tools include generating and editing inputs, finding real examples that strongly activate a component, and summarizing experimental results. MAIA combines these operations to investigate features rather than relying on a single observation. The approach matters because it automates parts of the experimental workflow used by human interpretability researchers.

The authors evaluate MAIA on computer vision models, including several trained models and synthetic neurons with known descriptions. Its neuron-level feature descriptions are comparable to those produced by expert human experimenters in these evaluations. They also show that MAIA can help reduce sensitivity to spurious features and identify inputs likely to receive incorrect predictions, connecting interpretation with practical diagnosis of model behavior.
icml-2024-a-multimodal-automated-interpr.tldr: MAIA uses a vision-language model and experimental tools to interpret visual features and help discover model failures.

paragraphs: Algorithm of Thoughts addresses the cost of making language models explore possible solutions. Some reasoning methods repeatedly stop generation, modify the search, and query the model again. The paper argues that this fragmented process increases query counts, token use, memory demands, and computation while giving the model a limited view of the overall exploration.

The proposed method places examples of algorithmic reasoning directly in the context. These examples guide the model through a more complete search process within one or a few queries. The aim is to use the model's own sequential generation dynamics to explore ideas, with the algorithmic examples providing structure for that exploration.

The reported results outperform earlier single-query approaches and more recent methods using extensive multi-query tree search, while consuming substantially fewer tokens. The authors also find evidence that a model guided by an algorithm can outperform that algorithm itself. They interpret this as suggesting that learned intuition can improve the search, rather than merely reproduce the demonstrated procedure.
icml-2024-algorithm-of-thoughts-enhancin.tldr: Algorithm of Thoughts uses in-context algorithmic examples to improve language-model search with fewer queries and tokens.

paragraphs: This paper studies prediction error when a model learns its final readout layer on top of an existing feature map. Its main result is a tight asymptotic characterization for a broad class of feature maps. The analysis considers a high-dimensional regime in which input size, hidden-layer widths, and training-sample count grow proportionally.

The characterization expresses test error through the population covariance of the features: the statistical relationships among feature values across the underlying data distribution. This makes feature covariance the central object connecting a representation to the performance of its learned readout. The result concerns this proportional-growth limit, rather than asserting an exact formula for every finite model.

The authors also analyze Gaussian rainbow networks, whose random weights have structure that can depend on earlier layers. For these networks, they derive an explicit feature-covariance formula from the weight matrices. They further find that their results can sometimes capture feature maps learned by finite-width networks trained with gradient descent, suggesting relevance beyond randomly constructed representations.
icml-2024-asymptotics-of-learning-with-d.tldr: The paper characterizes readout test error through feature covariance in a proportional high-dimensional limit, including structured random deep networks.

paragraphs: CLLM addresses tabular learning when only a small training dataset is available. Conventional synthetic-data generators must learn from that limited sample, which restricts the variety of useful examples they can produce. The paper instead draws on knowledge already contained in large language models to generate additional data for the downstream learning task.

Generation is paired with a curation mechanism because producing more rows does not automatically make a dataset more useful. The mechanism uses learning dynamics together with confidence and uncertainty measures to select higher-quality generated data. This makes the contribution a combination of data production and data assessment, with both parts directed toward improving downstream utility.

Across multiple real-world datasets, the authors report better performance than conventional generators in low-data settings. They also investigate the generation and curation mechanisms to understand what enables useful augmentation. The findings support the combined approach in the evaluated settings: a language model supplies potential examples, while curation helps determine which generated data should contribute to training.
icml-2024-curated-llm-synergy-of-llms-an.tldr: CLLM combines language-model-generated tabular data with learning-based curation to improve training when real data are scarce.

paragraphs: This paper asks how the internal parts of a machine learning model contribute to an individual prediction. It introduces component modeling, a framework that describes predictions in terms of architectural building blocks such as convolution filters and attention heads. The focus is on the model's internal computation as it transforms an input into an output.

The authors concentrate on component attribution, a specific version of that framework. Here, the goal is to estimate the counterfactual impact of an individual component on a prediction: how that prediction would be affected by changing the component's contribution. This gives the explanation a concrete target tied to the role of a particular internal part.

They introduce COAR as a scalable algorithm for estimating these attributions and demonstrate its effectiveness across models, datasets, and modalities. They also show that COAR enables effective model editing. Together, these results connect explaining a prediction with modifying the computation that produces it, giving component-level analysis a practical role beyond describing model behavior.
icml-2024-decomposing-and-editing-predic.tldr: COAR estimates how internal model components affect predictions and uses those attributions to support model editing.

paragraphs: Persistent homology provides descriptors of geometric structure that can be included in a learning objective. For a single real-valued function on geometric data, the standard descriptor is a barcode. Its mapping from function values is differentiable almost everywhere, and optimization using barcode-based losses already has a relatively well-developed theoretical foundation.

The situation becomes less unified when each data element has several function values. This multiparameter setting has many possible descriptors and no single canonical counterpart to the barcode. The paper develops a general framework for studying differentiability and optimization across a broad range of these descriptors, including signed barcodes and multiparameter persistence landscapes.

This framework gives several different ways of representing topology a common basis for optimization. Numerical experiments further support the possibility that optimizing multiparameter descriptors can improve performance over optimizing one-parameter descriptors. The reported benefit can occur even with simple, efficiently computable multiparameter descriptors, suggesting that richer topological information need not require the most elaborate available representation.
icml-2024-differentiability-and-optimiza.tldr: A general framework makes diverse multiparameter topological descriptors amenable to differentiation and optimization.

paragraphs: A learned solver needs enough computation to carry out the algorithm its task demands. This paper investigates that issue through the Differentiable Neural Computer, or DNC, a neural problem solver with external memory. The architecture allows the authors to examine how computational time and memory use relate to generalization.

The central variable is the planning budget: the number of planning steps available to the model. The authors argue that restricting this budget can impair generalization and prevent the model from fully using its external memory. Having storage available therefore does not by itself ensure that a learned solver has enough opportunities to use it effectively.

The study evaluates Graph Shortest Path, Convex Hull, Graph MinCut, and Associative Recall. Across these tasks, the planning budget can substantially change the learned algorithm's time complexity, training time, stability, and behavior on inputs larger than those used for training. The findings make computation allowance an important part of understanding a learned solver's behavior, alongside its memory capacity.
icml-2024-dncs-require-more-planning-ste.tldr: A DNC's planning budget can strongly affect its memory use, learned algorithm, and generalization to larger inputs.

paragraphs: Predicting another object's future motion involves uncertainty, so a trajectory model may represent several possible futures. Evaluating that output requires assessing the predicted distribution, not merely whether one candidate resembles the observed trajectory. This paper examines whether commonly used evaluation measures provide the right incentives for such uncertain predictions in autonomous systems.

The authors analyze the Minimum of N family of metrics through the framework of proper scoring rules. A strictly proper rule uniquely rewards reporting the true distribution in expectation. They show that Minimum of N lacks this property and demonstrate how it can therefore give a misleading assessment of predictions containing multiple possible trajectories.

As an alternative, the paper proposes evaluation measures based on the Energy Score, drawing on its established propriety. The significance is a closer connection between a favorable evaluation and an honest account of uncertainty. This contribution concerns how trajectory distributions are judged, providing a more reliable basis for assessing models whose outputs describe multiple plausible movements.
icml-2024-evaluation-of-trajectory-distr.tldr: The paper shows that Minimum of N can misjudge trajectory distributions and proposes proper Energy Score-based evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization using function evaluations instead of directly available gradients. Its focus is optimization over cross-polytopes, where existing methods become more costly as dimension increases. The main question is how much of that dimensional dependence can be reduced while retaining theoretical guarantees for the optimization procedure.

For bandit convex optimization with two-point feedback, the authors combine mirror descent with a symmetric negative one-half Tsallis entropy and an l1-ellipsoidal smoothing gradient estimator. The resulting dimensional dependence is O(sqrt(d)), improving on the previous O(sqrt(d log d)) dependence by a factor of sqrt(log d). The stated lower bound is Ω(sqrt(d/log d)), so the improvement does not close the entire known gap.

The authors also extend the idea to nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization, obtaining a convergence dependence of O(d), described as the best known. These results matter for gradient-free problems in which dimension is a major source of difficulty, including the paper's motivating applications in adversarial attacks, explainable AI, and sparse regression.
icml-2024-improved-dimensionality-depend.tldr: A mirror descent method improves the dimensional dependence of gradient-free convex optimization over cross-polytopes to O(sqrt(d)).

paragraphs: Weight-space learning trains neural networks to process the weights of other neural networks. Applications include reasoning about networks that represent images or three-dimensional scenes. The paper examines why these models often overfit and identifies limited diversity in their training datasets as an important empirical explanation for the problem.

One object can be represented by many different neural-network weight configurations. Typical datasets of implicit neural representations do not adequately capture this variation among networks representing the same object. The authors investigate augmentation strategies in weight space and introduce a version of MixUp adapted to these inputs, aiming to expose the learner to more varied weight representations.

The methods are evaluated in classification and self-supervised contrastive learning. In classification, their improvements are comparable to those obtained with up to ten times more data. In the contrastive setting, they produce reported downstream classification gains of 5–10%. The results support augmentation as a way to address insufficient representation diversity, with the stated benefits established in these evaluated setups.
icml-2024-improved-generalization-of-wei.tldr: Weight-space augmentation, including an adapted MixUp method, improves generalization by increasing the diversity of neural-network representations.

paragraphs: Federated training can be much slower than centralized training, making repeated tuning expensive. One way to reduce that burden is to simulate training on proxy data held by the server. Those simulations are useful only if they reflect the statistical differences among the real clients participating in federated learning.

A centralized proxy dataset usually has no natural division into clients. Splitting it naively can produce simulated clients whose data distributions differ from the real population, leading to misleading training dynamics. The paper addresses this partitioning problem with a fully federated algorithm that efficiently learns a distribution describing the true clients and has theoretical justification.

The inferred distribution is then used to divide centralized data into simulated clients. The authors observe improved server-side simulations when using these partitions. This matters because realistic simulations can support experimentation before costly runs on actual clients: the contribution improves how the proxy environment represents client heterogeneity, which is a key ingredient in making those experiments informative.
icml-2024-improved-modelling-of-federate.tldr: A federated algorithm learns client heterogeneity to create more realistic simulated clients from centralized proxy data.

paragraphs: This paper studies how language models change their beliefs as they receive feedback within a context. The authors use three instrumental learning tasks adapted from cognitive psychology. Their focus is whether outcomes that are better or worse than expected have equal influence on the model's subsequent learning and behavior.

In the studied tasks, the models learn more from better-than-expected outcomes than from worse-than-expected outcomes. However, the direction of this asymmetry reverses for counterfactual feedback, which concerns outcomes of alternatives to the action taken. The asymmetry also disappears when the task framing does not imply that the learner has agency.

The authors find similar patterns in idealized in-context learning agents obtained through meta-reinforcement learning. Together, these observations suggest that feedback processing depends substantially on how the learning problem is framed. The result is more specific than a general tendency toward optimism: the same kind of positive or negative surprise can have different influence depending on agency and the meaning of the feedback.
icml-2024-in-context-learning-agents-are.tldr: Language models update beliefs asymmetrically, with the direction and presence of that asymmetry depending on feedback and agency.

paragraphs: Language models are commonly trained with a logarithmic loss derived from maximum likelihood estimation. This loss corresponds to a strictly proper scoring rule: in expectation, the best forecast reports the true probabilities. Its local nature, depending only on the probability assigned to the observed sample, makes it practical for the enormous space of possible texts.

Other strictly proper scoring rules also encourage honest probabilities, but their nonlocal dependence creates a challenge for language generation. The paper proposes a strategy for adapting nonlocal scoring rules to this setting. It uses that strategy to train generation models with two established alternatives, the Brier score and the Spherical score.

The experiments indicate that replacing the loss while leaving other hyperparameters unchanged can substantially improve generation capabilities. The authors also report that these improvements can extend to LLaMA-7B and LLaMA-13B. The findings make the scoring rule itself a meaningful training choice, showing that the conventional logarithmic objective is not the only practically usable route to improved language generation.
icml-2024-language-generation-with-stric.tldr: Adapting nonlocal proper scoring rules lets language models train with Brier or Spherical losses, yielding reported generation improvements.

paragraphs: Learning a decision policy from recorded data is difficult when hidden confounders create misleading relationships between actions and outcomes. Instrumental-variable regression addresses this using an unconfounded variable called an instrument. The paper focuses on nonlinear, two-stage approaches that use neural networks to estimate causal relationships in this setting.

A common procedure directly inserts a first-stage estimate into the second-stage model. Errors from the first stage, particularly regularization bias, can then create substantial bias in the causal estimate. DML-IV introduces a new learning objective within the double/debiased machine learning framework to reduce this problem and support the learning of effective decision policies.

The authors establish strong convergence properties and an O(N^(-1/2)) policy suboptimality guarantee, matching the rate stated for unconfounded data. On instrumental-variable regression benchmarks, DML-IV outperforms leading comparison methods and learns high-performing policies when instruments are available. The contribution links bias reduction in causal estimation to policy quality, while retaining the instrumental-variable setting that makes learning from confounded data possible.
icml-2024-learning-decision-policies-wit.tldr: DML-IV reduces bias in nonlinear instrumental-variable regression and supports policy learning with O(N^(-1/2)) suboptimality guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper asks how communication frequency affects generalization in federated learning. It studies clients that periodically send local models to a parameter server for aggregation. The comparison holds each client's total training-data amount fixed: increasing the number of communication rounds means using less local training data in each round.

The authors derive PAC-Bayes and rate-distortion bounds that explicitly include communication rounds, client count, and dataset size. For federated support vector machines, a more explicit generalization bound grows with the number of rounds. This suggests that gains in training performance can outpace gains in population performance as communication becomes more frequent; the statement is about the bound and its implications.

The analysis also suggests a generalization-error advantage over centralized learning involving a factor of O(sqrt(log(K)/K)). Experiments with ResNet-56 provide evidence that the support-vector-machine observations may extend more broadly and that population risk may eventually rise with additional rounds. The findings challenge the expectation that more communication necessarily improves generalization under the paper's fixed-data setup.
icml-2024-lessons-from-generalization-er.tldr: With total client data fixed, theoretical bounds and experiments suggest that more federated communication can worsen generalization.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects from observational data often depends on assumptions that may fail in practice. This paper studies data collected across environments such as hospitals, physicians, or countries. It allows violations of both within-environment overlap and unconfoundedness, moving from a single identified conditional average treatment effect to bounds on that effect.

Under existing multiple-environment assumptions from the literature, the authors show that environment can be interpreted as an instrumental variable. This lets them adapt instrumental-variable bounds by using differences in how environments assign treatment. The approach makes those assignment differences useful for constraining possible treatment effects, even when the stated assumptions do not support a unique estimate.

The paper then develops model-agnostic meta-learners for estimating these bounds with arbitrary machine learning models. Experiments on simulated and real-world data demonstrate their effectiveness. The authors also discuss application to other partially identified instrumental-variable problems, including randomized trials with noncompliance. The practical output is an estimated range of effects that reflects the available identification information.
icml-2024-meta-learners-for-partially-id.tldr: Model-agnostic learners estimate treatment-effect bounds by using environments as instruments under stated multiple-environment assumptions.

paragraphs: MindEye2 reconstructs visual perception from brain activity while reducing the amount of training data needed from a new person. Earlier approaches train separately for each subject and can require dozens of hours of fMRI data. This work pretrains across seven subjects, then fine-tunes using only one hour from a new subject.

The method first uses linear mappings to align brain data into a shared representation across subjects. A shared nonlinear mapping then converts this representation into CLIP image space. To produce pixels, the authors fine-tune Stable Diffusion XL to accept CLIP representations instead of text, connecting the brain-derived image representation to image generation.

The authors report high-quality reconstructions with that limited new-subject data, improved generalization across subjects, and state-of-the-art retrieval and reconstruction metrics compared with single-subject approaches. The one-hour result relies on the prior training across other people. Its practical significance is that this shared learning can make accurate perception reconstruction possible from data gathered during a single MRI visit.
icml-2024-mindeye2-shared-subject-models.tldr: MindEye2 transfers learning across seven subjects to reconstruct visual perception using one hour of fMRI training data from a new subject.

paragraphs: This paper studies a bandit problem in which an available option can leave if the algorithm repeatedly neglects it. The setting is motivated by online advertising and crowdsourcing, where participants benefit only when selected. Choices therefore affect both the reward obtained now and which options remain available for future decisions.

The authors analyze the inherent difficulty of this setting and identify limitations of existing approaches. They propose FC-SE and establish upper bounds on its expected regret, the performance shortfall measured against the comparison used in the analysis. The guarantee addresses decision making when continued access to an option depends on giving it sufficient attention.

They then extend the problem to allow new options to arrive after the process has begun. A second algorithm, FC-Entry, comes with performance guarantees for that changing population. Experiments validate the theoretical findings. Together, the two algorithms address availability as part of the learning problem, accounting for participants who can exit and, in the extension, enter over time.
icml-2024-on-multi-armed-bandit-with-imp.tldr: FC-SE and FC-Entry provide guarantees for bandit learning when neglected options leave and new options may arrive.

paragraphs: Online experiments often use identifiers to connect what a person was shown with how that person later behaved. This becomes difficult when the same consumer uses several devices recorded under different identities. The resulting fragmented records can obscure the relationship between treatment exposure and outcomes, complicating estimates of preferences and causal effects.

The paper proposes HIFIVE, a variational method for estimating global average treatment effects from this incomplete view. Its target is the overall causal effect despite fragmented exposure and outcome records. The underlying challenge is not only estimation noise: without strong assumptions about the connections between users and devices, the causal effect may not be identifiable.

Experiments show that HIFIVE has lower bias and greater robustness to uncertainty about those connections than standard estimators. These findings support explicitly accounting for identity fragmentation when analyzing online experiments. They do not remove the stated identification issue; instead, the method offers an improved estimator for a setting where uncertain user-device relationships are central to the analysis.
icml-2024-on-online-experimentation-with.tldr: HIFIVE estimates global treatment effects from fragmented user-device records, with reported reductions in bias and improved robustness.

paragraphs: Foundation models can handle some distribution shifts well, but this paper finds that spurious correlations remain a problem. When training-time associations between labels and irrelevant features break at test time, zero-shot and few-shot performance is no better than empirical-risk-minimization models in the studied settings. Increasing pretraining data or model size leaves this performance unchanged.

The authors also observe that foundation models can accurately predict the spurious feature itself. A theoretical analysis in a simplified setting connects these findings to simplicity bias during contrastive pretraining: learned features tend to rely more on the spurious attribute than on robust alternatives. This diagnosis motivates using the model's ability to recognize that attribute.

Prompting for Robustness first predicts spurious attributes on labeled examples using zero-shot prompting. It then learns a classifier that balances performance across groups defined by labels and predicted attributes. Across five vision and language tasks, its performance nearly matches an oracle group-DRO method given human-labeled spurious attributes, showing how attribute prediction can support more robust classification.
icml-2024-prompting-is-a-double-edged-sw.tldr: Prompting for Robustness uses foundation-model predictions of spurious attributes to train classifiers with more balanced group performance.

paragraphs: Text-to-3D systems can draw on powerful image diffusion models, but strong image generation does not automatically provide consistent three-dimensional geometry. Fine-tuning on multiview datasets addresses this problem, yet the paper notes that available 3D data have less quality and diversity than 2D data. ReDream explores retrieval as another way to supply geometric knowledge.

The method retrieves assets that are semantically relevant and uses them directly during score-distillation optimization. The retrieved asset contributes a geometric prior to the variational objective. It also helps adapt the diffusion model's image prior toward consistency across views, connecting the expressive image model with structure supplied by an existing 3D asset.

The authors report substantial improvements in geometry and visual fidelity, with extensive experiments showing superior quality and increased geometric consistency. The approach matters because retrieval supplies relevant 3D information within the generation process itself. Its central proposal is to combine the strengths of image diffusion and 3D assets through optimization, rather than depending solely on multiview dataset fine-tuning.
icml-2024-retrieval-augmented-score-dist.tldr: ReDream uses retrieved 3D assets during score distillation to improve generated scenes' geometry, fidelity, and consistency across views.

paragraphs: MoNet is designed to learn end-to-end behavior while making its decision process more interpretable. The network uses functional modularity and a contrastive loss guided by latent representations to learn task-specific decision processes. These processes develop in the model's internal representation without requiring task-level supervision, linking self-supervised learning with a modular organization of behavior.

The method also includes an online, post-hoc explanation approach. It examines the learned system's inferences while preserving sensorimotor control performance. The authors investigate both perceptual saliency maps and latent decision vectors, providing two perspectives on interpretation: which perceptual information matters and how internal representations relate to decisions.

In real indoor environments, MoNet demonstrates effective autonomous navigation from visual input. It outperforms baseline models by 7% to 28% in task specificity analysis; that reported range concerns task specificity rather than a general navigation-success measure. The results show how modular learning and post-hoc analysis can work together to expose aspects of a robot's perception and behavior while maintaining control performance.
icml-2024-self-supervised-interpretable-.tldr: MoNet combines self-supervised modular learning with post-hoc explanations to make visual navigation decisions more interpretable.

paragraphs: Scientific simulators often combine several optional components, leaving researchers to decide both which components belong and what their parameters should be. Simulation-based model inference, or SBMI, tackles these choices jointly. It defines priors over candidate components and trains neural networks on simulations to infer distributions over model structure together with its associated parameters.

For component configurations, SBMI uses a conditional mixture of multivariate binary distributions expressed in the Grassmann formalism. This provides a representation for uncertainty about which components are included. The method applies to compositional stochastic simulators without evaluating likelihoods, making simulated outputs the basis for learning the joint inference procedure.

Evaluations use a simple time-series model and two neuroscience models. SBMI discovers multiple configurations consistent with the data and reveals components and parameters that are not identifiable. This matters because scientific evidence may support several explanations rather than one uniquely determined simulator. Representing those alternatives can help researchers judge which components are essential and make modeling decisions informed by uncertainty.
icml-2024-simultaneous-identification-of.tldr: SBMI jointly infers simulator components and parameters from simulations, exposing alternative explanations and non-identifiability.

paragraphs: The Balanced-Pairwise-Affinities transform changes a set of input features into representations that capture richer relationships among the items. Its goal is to help downstream tasks that match or group related examples. The transformed representation encodes higher-order relationships, making the structure of the feature set part of how each item is represented.

The construction starts from a fractional matching problem whose entropy-regularized version can be approximated using optimal transport. Its distinctive step is to match the feature set to itself and use rows of the resulting transport plan as the new features. The transform is efficient, differentiable, equivariant, parameterless, and has a probabilistic interpretation.

The authors report consistent improvements when inserting the transform into networks across varied tasks and training schemes. They demonstrate state-of-the-art results in few-shot classification, unsupervised image clustering, and person re-identification. These findings support the value of representing items through balanced relationships within the set, using a transform that can participate in learning without adding its own trainable parameters.
icml-2024-the-balanced-pairwise-affiniti.tldr: BPA turns self-matching optimal-transport relationships into parameterless features that improve several matching and grouping tasks.

paragraphs: SANE learns representations of trained neural networks by processing their weights. Earlier approaches struggled with larger models or focused on one type of task, such as discrimination or generation. This paper aims for representations that work across tasks and scale to larger networks with varying architectures, broadening what weight-space learning can support.

The key approach is to process subsets of weights sequentially. This extends hyper-representation learning by embedding a large network as a set of tokens in a learned representation space. The authors show that embeddings formed at the layer level reveal global information about the model, and that SANE can sequentially generate previously unseen neural networks.

In extensive empirical evaluations, SANE matches or exceeds state-of-the-art performance on several weight-representation benchmarks. The reported strengths are particularly evident in initialization for new tasks and larger ResNet architectures. The contribution combines a way to handle larger weight collections with evidence that the resulting representations support multiple uses, including understanding model properties and producing new models.
icml-2024-towards-scalable-and-versatile.tldr: SANE sequentially represents neural-network weights as tokens, supporting scalable model analysis, initialization, and generation.
